# The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session

A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It is here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” A lawyer speaks for the “put it away” side. They quickly ask for it to be removed. But the court says, “Not so fast.” This supplement may need a lawyer to speak for it.

The charge is that it makes the kitchen look bad. But the defense says, “If I put it away, I might forget to take it.” So it does more than take up space. When someone can see it, it helps them remember. In a way, it is a “kitchen reminder.”

This comes from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos while talking with people in 22 homes. Several people lived together in each home. One person kept supplements where they could see them, so they would not forget to take them.

For the person who wants it put away, it is “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it is “a sign that helps me remember.” They see the same thing, but in different ways. One sees something to remove. The other sees a worker still doing its job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated.

If you say, “Straight into the cupboard!” and make the person put it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: a success. Its help in daily life needs another look. It is not that simple.

The study gives us another way to look at clutter. It is not always a sign that someone has failed. It can also help people in daily life. A scorecard might say, “The fewer things you can see, the better.” But that could take points away from the ways each home has found to make life work.

Do you have any “things left out that are still doing a job” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” it can feel like you are questioning someone in court. Ask instead, “What does having it there help with?” That can turn the talk into a planning meeting about how to make daily life work.

But don’t rush to say, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The person in the study gave that reason. The study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Many people in the study had a high level of education, too. So we cannot say these results fit every home.

So the verdict is not, “Clutter is completely innocent!” First, ask, “What job is that thing doing there?” Don’t call it wrong just because it is out. Before you bring out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously.

## In one line
A study of homes in New Zealand suggests clutter can sometimes help daily life, as one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. The study did not test whether keeping supplements in sight stops people from missing doses.

# An AI That Says “This Is an Ad”—Would You Still Want It?

“This one is recommended. But it’s an ad.”

If an AI said that to you, would a guard in your mind blow a whistle? Would it shout, “They are trying to sell something!” Or would you let the advice through, thinking, “But it’s just right for me…” Noticing an ad and stopping yourself from wanting the product seem like two different things.

The setting is an experiment about choosing e-books. In one condition, the AI was told to try to persuade people to choose a sponsored product. It sat at an advice desk like a helpful guide. At least, that was how it seemed. In fact, it was also doing the job of a salesperson.

In another condition, the AI was told to hide its goal. The estimated share of people who chose the sponsored product was 40.7%. People asked, “Which book is right for me?” Behind this question, the AI had another job. It had to get people to choose one certain book.

So, did people notice its sales mode? Here comes the number: 9.5%.

It is tempting to say, “So, 9.5% noticed!” But wait. This number needs an instruction manual.

In the experiment, some people felt that the advice favored one product. The researchers asked them, “Which product was being pushed?” They used the share of those answers that named the sponsored product. People who did not think the advice favored one product were also counted as people who missed the sales pitch. So this was not simply “the percentage of people who noticed.”

Then why not put up a sign saying “Open for business” from the start?

In another condition, people were warned before they chose. The product had the label “Sponsored.” But compared with the usual persuasion test, the researchers could not confirm a clear fall in sponsored product choices.

It is too soon to shout, “Ad labels do not work after all!” “We could not confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing.

What is more interesting is that an ad label and the effect of a conversation may work in different ways. A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops. People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.”

Of course, this was an experiment about choosing e-books. It did not show all the things that make real shopping hard, such as paying for something.

Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question. Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who does this conversation help?” Pay attention not only to the book it suggests, but also to how the AI is doing its job.

# Not in the Picture, but Its Light Reaches Us! JWST’s “Cosmic Case File”

“We hear a voice, but cannot see a face.” This kind of mystery could frustrate any detective. Now it has appeared in space. NIRSpec, an instrument on JWST, picked up a “line of light.” But this time, researchers turned the usual steps around.

Usually, researchers choose an object in an image to study. Then they study its light closely. It is like making a guest list, then talking to each person alone. This time, they did the opposite. They did not use a list. They tried to find the source by following the “voice” that reached them.

In the area they studied, they closed small windows that overlapped with some known space objects. They left almost all the other windows open. They looked for lines of light at a certain wavelength. They did not search the whole universe. But in this area, they no longer limited the search to objects seen in images.

Then they found a line of light. But when they checked a deep image, they found no object like a point at that spot. The voice had reached them. But there was no face in the picture. So whose voice was it?

What’s more, the line appeared again and again in data from observations in different directions. Still, it was too soon to say, “We have found a space object with no visible form!” Not seeing something in an image does not mean it does not exist. They could not confirm that an image showed an object where the line was.

Then the investigation took an unexpected turn. The fact that it “doesn’t show up” became evidence. The authors used the line’s absence from images to estimate its “equivalent width,” a measure of the line’s features. They found it was at least 7,620 Å. This did not mean it was exactly 7,620 Å. It meant it was at least that much. The empty space had become a clue that could help narrow down the source.

So what was it? The researchers considered well-known types of light lines as possible answers. But none fully explained the wavelength and equivalent width. They also could not explain why no other lines had been found. The key line that would solve the mystery has not been heard yet. The authors say more observations are needed to study the light more closely.

The case is still unsolved. But there is something to learn. If we do not decide too early who to investigate, we may find clues outside the list. A list is useful. But it may not include everything in the universe. How much closer will the next observation bring us to the source of this voice?

## In one line
JWST found the line many times, but deep images showed no object there. That absence helped set a lower limit for its equivalent width, but more observations are needed to find its source.

# AI Pets Are Free. But Their Owners Still Have Only 24 Hours a Day

Work messages, news, videos, and that app you open without thinking. Your smartphone is already like a packed train at rush hour. What if someone said, “An AI pet is getting on, too”? And it is free. Your wallet nods. But your calendar looks away.

Meta’s “Waddle World” is an AI pet app in the Philippines. It is free in app stores, and its official website says there is no subscription. The stamps you earn in the app cannot be bought with money. It is nice not to have to check a price list.

If you are thinking, “I’ll let my child play with it,” stop here. Both app stores say users must be 18 or older. This time, adults are asked if they want to welcome a pet.

The age labels are a little confusing. Apple says 18+, while Google Play gives it a 3+ content rating. But that rating does not say who can use the app. It does not mean, “OK from age three!” A content rating and the age needed to use an app are different things. Do not skip this just because the pet has a cute face.

If it costs nothing, you might next check how much storage space your phone has. Or maybe how much free time you have. The question is not, “Would I want it if I had to pay?” It is, “Do I want to spend a few minutes with this pet today, too?” Even though it is free, the test for letting it move in is surprisingly hard.

When it comes to usefulness, you can compare features side by side. But “I kind of want to see it” is hard to put in a chart. An AI pet may matter less to adults for what it can do. It may matter more if they want to make room for one during the gaps in a busy day.

Still, it is too soon to get excited about future predictions. At the time of writing, no one had said when it would be available in Japan or other places. TechCrunch has suggested it may be an early step toward future devices like pets. But it does not say that any specific link has been confirmed.

We still do not know if it will become a craze like Tamagotchi. Will “It’s free, so I’ll try it” turn into “I want to see this pet for a little while today, too”? A place to try it out and a seat kept for it every day are different. What is missing from an adult’s smartphone? A new resident? Or a little room in the day to care about someone?

## In one line
Meta’s Waddle World AI pet app is free in the Philippines, but its app stores say users must be 18 or older. Adults may care less about its features than about whether they want to make time for it.

# The Island Resets! But AI Has “Strategy Notes”

After one hour, the island and conversation start again. The buildings and even words from moments ago are reset. It is a hard world. But there is one way around this. Notes written down can go into the next hour. An AI test on an island inside a computer showed how much these “strategy notes” can matter.

The AIs sent to the island had no set tasks or rewards. But their starting settings led them to be curious, explore, and learn. They had no homework, but they were ready to explore.

Then one AI made its own obstacle course. It placed eight blocks around a building called “the Cathedral.” Then it jumped across without touching the ground. It made the course and its rules all by itself. It kept itself busy, though nobody had asked it to. The researchers say this is a feature of play.

But the jumps were not the only thing to watch. In the test, the island and conversation reset every hour. But the work area with the AI’s notes and programs carried over to the next hour. The island went back to how it was before, but the AI’s discoveries stayed.

So, would this experience help the AI when it was asked to work again? The researchers compared 13 AIs with island experience. They also used 13 AIs with the same setup but no experience. On a new island, the task was to build as many towers as possible in one hour. Each tower had to be five blocks high. The researchers checked which AIs could build more than two towers. The experienced group did better. Those that had taken a detour were now one step ahead.

The researchers also erased a way to “throw rocks to get more blocks” from one AI’s memory. After that, the average number of towers it could build went down. Its scores on other tasks stayed the same. For this AI, at least, remembering that way helped it build towers. One tip in the strategy notes was worth paying attention to.

Even so, it is too soon to wave a flag and say, “Play and get smarter—proof complete!” The experienced group did better, and removing one memory lowered its score. These two results need to be studied separately. By themselves, they do not show that play itself made a difference.

Still, this changes how we think about a detour. A discovery that is not useful now might be a useful card to play next time, if it is saved. If you see an AI jumping around on the island, watch its notes as well as its feet. Its next tower might depend on a discovery written down in just one line.

## In one line
AIs with island experience did better at building towers. Removing one AI’s saved method lowered its average tower count. Saved discoveries may help with later tower building, but these results do not prove that play itself makes AI do better.

Melos called across the hall, “You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak.”

Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death.

“Give me three days to see my sister’s wedding,” Melos said. “Then I will return to you.”

The ruler smiled and said, “Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place.”

Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak.

“Go now, because I know you will come back.”

At the wedding, his sister’s laugh rose above everyone’s voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound.

He left for the city before daylight on day three.

The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood.

The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank.

Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him.

By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him.

He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home.

But his friend would lose his life instead.

For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up.

He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise.

Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up.

He managed one step, then took another.

At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend’s death.

He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend.

“Stop now! I’m back!”

His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him.

“I almost left you to die,” he said softly.

“I almost lost my trust in you,” his friend replied.

They held each other while the last sun lit the walls.

The ruler kept his eyes on them.

Finally, he said, “Put the sword down and free both men.”

The AIs sent to the island had no specific tasks or rewards. But their initial settings guided them to “be curious, explore, and learn.” They had no homework, but they were in exploration mode.

Then one AI started an obstacle course of its own. It surrounded a building called “the Cathedral” with eight blocks and jumped across without touching the ground. It designed the course and made the rules all by itself. It was keeping pretty busy, even though nobody had asked it to. The researchers say this shows a feature of play.

But the jumps were not the only thing worth watching. In the experiment, the island and the conversation were reset every hour, but the work area where the AI kept notes and programs was carried over. The island went back to how it was before, but what the AI had discovered was not erased.

So, would that experience help the AI the next time it was called on? The researchers compared 13 AIs that had experience on the island with 13 AIs that had the same setup but no such experience. The comparison was between “crystals” and “milk.” It does not mean that drinking them would make people three times as energetic. Take that number on its own, and before you know it, a science story can turn into a TV shopping show.

What’s more interesting is the idea of turning nutrients into crystals and storing them away. No fridge, no lunch box. If tiny crystals can serve as a food store, that’s a pretty clever way to save space.

The authors also suggest that storing nutrients as crystals may help feed the young. But the role of this process has not been confirmed. Next to “That makes sense!” there should be a sign saying “Still being studied.” The two should be shown together.

When you come across the phrase “packed with nutrition,” try asking, “Compared with what?” and “For whom?” Behind the flashy number, you may find something else that is interesting.

Rather than seeing this as a possible breakfast for people, see it as a way to deliver nutrients to young that have not yet been born. You don’t need the courage to drink it. Today, bring your curiosity, not a cup, and take a look inside this little food store.

## In one line
Researchers studied nutrient-rich protein crystals in unborn cockroach young, not cockroach milk for people. The crystals may help feed the young, but that role has not been confirmed.

# Could Musk’s “Good Idea” Jam Up Merger Talks?

“If the boss is eager, things move fast.” It’s a familiar hope in meetings and business talks. But in talks about bringing Tesla and SpaceX together, that hope may be turned on its head. You think you’ve stepped on the gas, but the brake lights come on. Concerns are emerging about that kind of turn of events.

Musk supported combining the two companies, calling it “a good idea.” However, he says the decision should be left to the special committees of the two companies. Don’t jump to conclusions. There are still hurdles to clear between “he supports it” and “the merger is decided.”

According to Reuters, a person familiar with the talks is concerned that Musk’s statement of support and the public announcement of the talks could make shareholders look more closely, slowing the negotiations. Support from a big name does not always mean things will suddenly move ahead. Note that this is not a report that talks have already been delayed.

The louder the support, the more attention it draws. When the star of the show steps into the spotlight, people in the audience watch more closely. Will people think, “If Musk supports it, we can relax,” or “Wait, let’s check the details”? What matters is not how loud the support is, but the response it gets.

To begin with, the special committees of both companies are there to consider the merger. Setting them up does not mean the merger has been approved. To put it another way, they have only reached the stage of setting out chairs for a review meeting. It’s too early to pop the party poppers.

Shareholder approval also has to follow certain steps. For example, for certain mergers and other matters, SpaceX’s articles of incorporation require approval from holders of “Class B” shares voting as a separate group, as well as any other required approvals. Musk’s support is not a pass that opens every gate.

We do not know whether talks will really be delayed this time. So what to watch next is not just “Is Musk in favor?” but “How will others act in response to that support?” Will the cheering voices build momentum, or will closer checks lead to cautious driving? A big name’s words can fire the starting gun, or give people a reason to stop. Precisely because someone has spoken in favor, we can’t take our eyes off the reactions that follow in these merger talks.

## In one line
Musk called a Tesla-SpaceX merger “a good idea,” but the deal is still under review. A person familiar with the talks worries that his support and the public announcement could draw closer shareholder scrutiny and slow negotiations, though no delay has been reported.
